set.approach: Drive the Halfmoon Creek dirt road about five miles west of Leadville to the large North Mount Elbert trailhead, a little over 10,000 feet; the lot fills early on weekends. Walk south into the forest, turn left onto the Colorado Trail over a footbridge, and switchback for about a mile. Turn right at the signed junction onto the North Elbert Trail, reach treeline near 11,900 feet, then climb to the northeast ridge crest around 12,700 feet where the climbing proper begins.
set.descent_text: Retrace the northeast ridge trail to the trailhead. Shortly below the summit you pass the junction for the East Ridge trail; stay on the northeast ridge path so you do not drop onto the wrong route. The steep, rocky stretch between about 13,800 and 13,400 feet deserves care on the way down, and the same switchbacks and Colorado Trail section lead back to the car.
hazards: Steep rocky section between roughly 13,400 and 13,800 feet where the trail braids and is hard to follow
Afternoon lightning on the long, bare northeast ridge above treeline
Wrong-trail risk at the East Ridge junction just below the summit on descent
Heavy weekend crowding and a trailhead lot that fills early

review.notes: Season from the general summer 14er window; the route page itself states none.

set.overview: The standard trail route up Colorado's third-highest summit, a long and mostly nontechnical Class 2 day through the Mount Massive Wilderness. It follows a good path through forest, willows and tundra to the 13,900-foot saddle that links the main summit with South Massive, then picks along the rocky crest past a notch and a false summit to the top. The distance, not the difficulty, is the crux.
set.approach: Drive the Halfmoon Creek dirt road west of Leadville for about five miles to the Mount Massive trailhead at roughly 10,080 feet. Leave on the Colorado Trail and Mount Massive Trail, crossing South Willow Creek near two miles and Willow Creek about a mile later. Climb northwest to a junction near 11,300 feet and turn left onto the Mount Massive Trail, which crosses clearings and willows to treeline and the open slopes where the real climb begins.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came: down the summit ridge to the notch and 13,900-foot saddle, then the trail through the willows and clearings back to the Colorado Trail junction near 11,300 feet. Stay right of the crest on the upper ridge, and at the notch near 14,250 feet watch for the junction with the Southwest Slopes route so you do not take it by mistake.
hazards: Rocky summit ridge with a false summit and moderate exposure near the top
Rockfall potential from other parties on the upper slopes and ridge
Afternoon lightning above treeline on the exposed east slopes
Long day with two stream crossings that run high in early summer

evidence.fact: 13.75 miles round trip; halved to 6.875 miles one-way = 11.07 km

review.notes: Distance single-source. Season is general summer 14er window.

set.overview: The standard route up the third-highest peak in the Sawatch, a long Class 2 climb through the Collegiate Peaks Wilderness. It follows a good trail up Horn Fork Basin to a talus section and shoulder near 13,000 feet, then switchbacks to the south ridge and follows its right side to the summit. The final pitch is the crux, on mostly stable rock, with an easier line that keeps it at Class 2.
set.approach: Take the dirt county road west from Buena Vista to the North Cottonwood Creek trailhead at the road end, about 9,900 feet. Pick up the trail on the parking loop’s west edge, cross a bridge, then follows the creek about 1.4 miles to a second bridge. Stay right at the junction for Horn Fork Basin and Bear Lake, keep left at the Mount Columbia junction, and reach treeline near 11,500 feet where the open basin begins.
set.descent_text: Descend the same way: down the south ridge switchbacks and cairned slope to the talus section and shoulder near 13,000 feet, then into Horn Fork Basin. Stay left at the Bear Lake junction on the way down, and keep following the creek trail through the junctions back to the trailhead. Take the talus slowly, as the footing is loose.
hazards: Rugged loose talus section below the 13,000-foot shoulder
Crux final pitch near the summit with loose rock and route-finding
Afternoon lightning on the open basin and exposed south ridge
Long approach and descent make a late start risky

evidence.fact: 13.75 miles round trip from North Cottonwood trailhead; one-way 6.875 mi = 11.07 km

review.notes: Distance single-source. Season is general window.

set.overview: A narrow couloir on the north side of Blanca, between the main peak and Ellingwood Point, climbed first in May 2008. It is about 1,500 feet of alpine ice and mixed ground, with roughly 1,100 feet of ice: an easy first pitch, a steepening gully, a snow ramp, then about 600 feet of 50 to 55 degree ice with an 80 degree step. Rated WI3 M5, Grade IV, in the Sangre de Cristo Wilderness.
hazards: Upper gully faces the sun, so ice and snow soften and shed
Rotten ice in the right branch of the upper couloir
Sustained steep ice with an 80 degree step and thin protection
Long wilderness approach and a descent that needs rappels and a glissade

review.notes: Skipped gain, distance and season: no page opened gives them for this route (page gives no season; only the first ascent was in May).

set.overview: The long, jagged ridge on the far side of La Plata Basin, a roughly two-mile traverse mostly near 13,000 feet. The climbing is mostly sustained Class 3 with sections of Class 4, and it can be pushed to easy 5th class if the crest is followed strictly; difficulties can be bypassed on the east side. After the ridge, a climb of about 1,300 feet leads to a false summit and a short walk to the true top. About 10 miles and 5,200 feet in total.
set.approach: Park on the Highway 82 side toward Independence Pass and walk the dirt road past a large bridge; the first mile crosses private land with a sign-in station. Follow the trail past a smaller bridge to a third creek, then take the left fork at a small rise (the right fork is the Northwest Ridge descent). Follow the faint trail about 1.5 miles to a fourth creek, go up it about 1,000 feet, cross, and climb roughly 1,200 feet of loose talus to the ridge shoulder.
set.descent_text: Descend the standard Northwest Ridge trail, a Class 2 path that is well marked once you leave the talus near the top. It runs back down to the junction near the third creek, where the right fork you passed on the way in joins, then follows the approach trail and road to the car. Allow a long day; the whole loop takes around eight hours car to car for a fast party.
hazards: Loose rock throughout; test every hold on the ridge
Lightning on the long, exposed crest, with difficult escape routes
Tiring, ankle-twisting talus fields on the approach
Faint approach trail and route-finding on the crest
Creek water carries mine metals, so carry your own

review.notes: Page names the Lake Creek trailhead while the row waypoint says La Plata trailhead on Highway 82; wrote it neutrally. Season general.

set.approach: From Lake City follow the Henson Creek road of the Alpine Loop about five miles to the Nellie Creek trail sign, then take the rough narrow 4WD road for about four miles with two creek crossings to the trailhead at roughly 11,400 feet. Without a high-clearance 4WD, park on Henson Creek road and walk, adding about 4,000 feet of gain round trip. From the upper lot, climb half a mile to treeline and follow Nellie Creek into the basin south of the peak.
set.descent_text: Reverse the route: down the loose Class 2 section past the rock tower and the steep west-face crux, along the trail to the south ridge near 13,800 feet, then across the basin to the junction near 11,950 feet. Follow Nellie Creek down to the trailhead. Take the loose 150-foot crux slowly and keep clear of other parties below you.
hazards: A short band of steep, loose rock, roughly 150 feet tall, on the west face just under the summit slopes
Considerable rockfall on the crux and loose Class 2 terrain
Early-season stream crossings on the Nellie Creek 4WD road
Lightning on the open ridge and summit plateau

set.approach: Drive from Westcliffe to the South Colony Lakes road and continue to the 4WD trailhead near 9,950 feet (the 2WD trailhead adds about 2.7 miles each way). Hike toward Lower South Colony Lake and, near 11,650 feet, turn left toward Broken Hand Pass at about 12,900 feet, with a Class 3 section below it. Descend west past Cottonwood Lake and traverse around cliffs to a bench, then reach the base of the Red Gully near 13,100 feet.
set.descent_text: Climb back down from the summit ledges to the notch at 14,150 feet, then reverse the Red Gully. Downclimb its red rock carefully, as it is steep in places. Return to the bench and Cottonwood Lake, climb to Broken Hand Pass at about 12,900 feet, and descend the loose slope to the trail at South Colony Lakes and the trailhead.
hazards: Considerable rockfall in the Red Gully, especially with other parties above
Exposed Class 3 conglomerate ledges near the summit
Loose, steep ground and a Class 3 section below Broken Hand Pass
Water running in the gully and lingering snow early in the season
Long day with a late descent through route-finding terrain

evidence.fact: 13.5 miles round trip from the 4WD trailhead; one-way 6.75 mi = 10.86 km

review.notes: Distance measured from 4WD trailhead (matches stored 6,200 ft gain). Season general.

set.overview: The standard route up Mount Lincoln is a Class 2 loop over neighbouring summits rather than a single ridge: from Kite Lake it crosses Mount Democrat's east slope to the saddle with Cameron, follows Cameron's west ridge, then drops to the Cameron-Lincoln saddle and finishes on a final Class 2 pitch. It is short, about six miles round trip, but gains and loses height across three high points.
set.approach: From Alma on Colorado 9, follow the small road sign on the west side of town through a residential area and continue about six miles to Kite Lake at 12,000 feet; the last mile is rougher but passable for a good-clearance car when dry, and there is a day-use fee. Walk the closed road past the lake, climb out of the basin, pass a collapsed mine shack near 12,200 feet and take the trail to the base of Democrat's east side.
set.descent_text: Return over the same summits in reverse: back across the Cameron-Lincoln saddle and Cameron, down to the Democrat-Cameron saddle near 13,400 feet, then across Democrat's east slope and down the rugged slope near 12,600 feet. Pass the mine shack and follow the closed road past the lake to the Kite Lake lot.
hazards: Rugged loose slope below Mount Democrat's east side
Moderate rockfall and exposure on the final Class 2 pitch
Lightning on the open ridges above 14,000 feet
Road to Kite Lake can be wet or snowy early in the season

review.notes: Distance is for the loop over Democrat and Cameron; single-source. The page gives no descent, so the descent is the reverse of the stated ascent. Season general.

set.overview: The usual route up Castle Peak is a Difficult Class 2 climb from Castle Creek in the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness. It follows an old mining road up Montezuma Basin, climbs a snow-prone headwall of about 500 feet, then takes a faint trail to the northeast ridge near 13,700 feet. The ridge leads to a small saddle and a steep, loose final pitch of roughly 250 feet with some route-finding.
set.approach: From the roundabout west of Aspen, drive about 12.5 paved miles up Castle Creek Road, then onto Forest Road 102, where passenger cars can go about a mile to dispersed camping. Walk or drive the road to a footbridge crossing near 10,200 feet, stay right at the Pearl Pass junction near 11,150 feet, and continue up Montezuma Basin to the road end at about 12,800 feet past the Montezuma Mine.
hazards: Headwall near 12,800 feet that keeps snow into late summer
Steep loose final pitch with rocky sections needing route-finding
Creek crossing near 10,200 feet that runs high in spring and early summer
Lightning above treeline on the open ridge

review.notes: Season general; headwall snow note kept.

set.overview: The most popular Class 1 route to the 14,270-foot summit, following a well-built trail up Stevens Gulch from the Grays Peak trailhead near 11,250 feet. The trail rises steadily across an open basin, reaches a junction near 13,300 feet where the right branch goes to Torreys Peak, and finishes with switchbacks across the upper north slope. It is about 7.5 miles round trip.
set.approach: Take Interstate 70 to the Bakerville exit and drive south toward Forest Road 189, where a lot serves as the winter trailhead; low-clearance cars should park here. In summer a rough road continues almost three miles to the Grays Peak trailhead near 11,280 feet. From the lot a footbridge crosses the Stevens Gulch creek, and the main trail heads on toward the basin and the saddle.
set.descent_text: Descend the same trail: down the switchbacks and north slope to the junction near 13,300 feet, where you stay on the Grays branch back toward Stevens Gulch. Follow the gentle trail across the flat rocky area near 12,300 feet to the information sign and the bridge, then to the trailhead. In winter add the road walk back to the I-70 exit.
hazards: Winter avalanche paths on the southeast side of Kelso Mountain that can run over the trail
Lightning above treeline on the open ridge and summit
Rough access road that needs a high-clearance vehicle in summer
Crowds and trail congestion on summer weekends

review.notes: Season general. The crowds hazard is not in the page; it is general popularity.

set.overview: The standard way up Antero is a long Class 2 climb that mostly follows old mining jeep roads from Baldwin Gulch to the west slopes, then crosses to the south ridge. Higher up, the ridge crest and trail segments past an old mining area give the most engaging terrain, and a final steep pitch leads from the 13,850-foot saddle to the summit. It is about 15.5 miles round trip.
set.approach: From US 285 south of Buena Vista, drive west on Chaffee County Road 162 toward Mount Princeton for about 12.5 miles, the last 2.5 on dirt, to the Baldwin Gulch jeep road (277) on the left. Park at the pull-offs near 9,400 feet. Follow the 277 road about three miles to a junction at 10,850 feet, turn left onto road 278 over Baldwin Creek, and continue about 1.5 miles to treeline and the west slopes.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent: down the south ridge past the old mining area, back along the 278A and 278 jeep roads to the junction at 10,850 feet, then the 277 road to the car. The final pitch's eroded side trail traverses right and gives poor footing, so downclimbing the ridge crest itself is the better line. A high-clearance vehicle shortens the day by driving part of the road.
hazards: Eroded traverse trail on the final pitch
Ridge-crossing sections with snow patches that linger into June
Rough steep jeep road that needs a capable high-clearance vehicle
Lightning on the exposed ridge above 13,000 feet

review.notes: Season Jul-Sep because the page says snow covers the lower road until early July.

hazards: Avalanche terrain on the standard approach, which has caught skiers and climbers
Rockfall on the face, which makes booting up it unwise
Steep choke over 40 degrees that sets the difficulty
Runouts beneath Kelso Mountain that call for route changes
Winter road closure at the I-70 exit makes for a very long day

review.notes: Skipped distance and season: no page gives a trailhead-to-summit distance for this route, and season is only stated as winter and spring. The on-foot descent sentence is an inference from the standard Grays/Torreys trail.
